Subject: Post-call: Performance SLOs & Autoscaling / Next steps

Tom — thanks for the time this morning. Quick recap and proposed next steps from our discovery focused on latency/throughput SLOs and autoscaling behavior. Please correct anything I got wrong.

High-level: Acme is planning to embed real-time personalization in the checkout flow. Primary SLOs we captured:
- P95 latency target: <= 150ms for single-turn text generation (non-streaming)
- Streaming target: average token-latency <= 50ms (server-to-client streaming) for conversational flows
- Sustained throughput target: 200 req/s at 1k token avg; expected peak bursts up to 1k req/s for 30-90s windows
- Concurrent sessions to support: ~300 active concurrent inference contexts (KV cache retained per session)

Autoscaling and availability requirements:
- Burst tolerance: app must absorb sudden 3-5x traffic spikes with minimal degradation to P95 (acceptable graceful degradation: increase to 250ms for up to 60s)
- Cold-start tolerance: want scale-up times < 2 minutes for cold capacity, and < 30s for warm pool activation
- Queueing behavior: prefer bounded queueing with backpressure to caller and predictable 95th latency when autoscaling is happening

Immediate next steps we agreed on:
1) Redwood to propose a scale policy and warm-pool sizing plan (attachment: scale_policy_proposal.pdf).
2) Vivek to confirm expected scale-up times for both Dedicated and Hosted modes and note any streaming-specific differences.
3) Acme to share a representative short load-run (30–60s) or synthetic traffic profile we can use for a pilot.
4) Align on a 2-hr pilot window to validate P95 and burst behavior.

Attachments: scale_policy_proposal.pdf (draft)

Thanks — I'll sync internally and loop back with more detail and a proposed pilot calendar.

—Marissa

Tom / Marissa — high level technical answers and items we'll validate in the pilot. TL;DR: Dedicated + warm pools can meet your targets with the right sizing; streaming behavior is lower-latency but has different scale characteristics. Details below.

1) Scale-up times (typical ranges):
- Cold new instance provisioning (cold scale): 60–120s depending on GPU type and instance boot time (includes model load/compile).
- Warm pool activation (pre-warmed instances with model in memory): typically < 20–30s to route traffic and start serving; in our Dedicated offering we can keep a warm pool sized to your expected burst capacity.
- Horizontal autoscale within an already warmed pool: near-instant (sub-second routing) to additional warmed nodes if capacity is available.

2) Warm pool design options we recommend for Acme:
- Option A (conservative): Maintain warm pool sized for 50% of expected peak (500 req/s) + autoscale for remaining. This reduces exposure to cold scale events and keeps cost moderate.
- Option B (aggressive): Keep warm pool sized for full expected peak bursts (1k–1.5k req/s). Highest cost but minimizes latency variance.

3) Queueing and backpressure behavior:
- By default Redwood uses bounded request queues at the route level. When capacity is saturated we return 429s with an explicit Retry-After header. For many apps we expose a token-based queueing policy that ensures requests are accepted only up to a configured in-flight limit to avoid head-of-line blocking.
- During scale-up we prioritize in-flight requests on warmed capacity and route new requests to queue/backpressure. We can also configure request prioritization per-route (e.g., checkout priority high).

4) Streaming differences:
- Streaming reduces perceived latency for clients (first token delivered), but sustained token throughput still requires the same model CPU/GPU work. For streaming-heavy flows we size warm pools based on concurrent streaming sessions rather than requests/sec. A single streaming session can hold a slot for longer depending on tokens produced.

5) Telemetry and pilot instrumentation we need from Acme:
- Request/response sample (JSON) + auth headers format.
- Representative token counts for prompts and expected responses.
- Traffic profile (per-second counts) for a 10-minute high-volume slice.
- SLOs/alert thresholds you want us to evaluate during the pilot (P95, P99, error rate, token-latency for streaming).

6) Pilot plan we propose:
- Redwood sets up a dedicated pool with warm instances sized per Option A.
- Run a 2-hr pilot on 2026-02-18. During the pilot we'll run synthetic bursts up to your peak and collect P95/P99 and streaming token-latency.
- We'll provide an instrumentation dashboard (per-route P95/P99, cost per 1k tokens, queueing events, 429 counts) and deliver a short write-up with recommended final sizing.

Attached: acme_latency_snapshot.csv — a quick sample from a similar pilot for a retail customer (sanitized).

Happy to jump on a 30-min pre-pilot tech sync if you want to walk through the warm-pool tuning.

—Vivek
